This was a very cool feature and one of my favorite toys growing up so I decided, since the original product is long gone after having grown, I should design a 3D printable replica to revive this old memory.

## Design

### 2026-10-16 – It all started with a wave of pure childhood nostalgia. While brainstorming ideas for the upcoming Half Life Event, I found myself reminiscing about my absolute favorite toy growing up: a classic, lig

**2h**

It all started with a wave of pure childhood nostalgia. While brainstorming ideas for the upcoming Half Life Event, I found myself reminiscing about my absolute favorite toy growing up: a classic, lightweight plastic Star Wars lightsaber that could magically telescope outward with a quick flick of the wrist and collapse right back down into a compact hilt. Long since lost or broken over the years, I realized that this event was the ultimate excuse to resurrect that memory. Instead of buying a replica, I set out to design a fully 3D-printable version from scratch, translating an old childhood wonder into a modern CAD project.

Before touching any CAD software, I spent an evening at my desk with a sketchbook mapping out the proportions. The math behind a multi-stage collapsing blade turned out to be surprisingly intricate; every millimeter counts when things have to nest inside one another. I started by defining the constraints: the hilt needed to be a comfortable 200 millimeters, while the fully extended blade should reach roughly 800 millimeters to feel proportional. Working backward from that target length, I calculated the ideal number of concentric segments—four telescoping layers—ensuring there was a precise 15 millimeter overlap between each stage. This overlap is crucial because it provides structural rigidity when extended, keeping the blade from sagging while preventing the pieces from sliding past each other.

The real heart of the design came down to the physical mechanics of the saber columns. Injection-molded toys achieve this smoothly, but engineering it for FDM 3D printing required clever geometry. I hand-drew cross-sections featuring internal retaining lips and a slight, tapered conical flare at the base of each segment. These tapered stops act as mechanical locks: when you flick the saber open, centrifugal force drives each column outward until the lips catch securely against the next layer, locking them in place without jamming. Dialing in the tolerances in my sketches—leaving just enough clearance for smooth sliding without making the blade wobbly—was the final hurdle before finally jumping into the CAD workspace.

### 2026-10-16 – With the conceptual dimensions settled, I moved the project into SolidWorks to bring the design into a digital workspace. Starting with a wireframe ghost view, I mapped out the precise concentric circ

**3h**

With the conceptual dimensions settled, I moved the project into SolidWorks to bring the design into a digital workspace. Starting with a wireframe ghost view, I mapped out the precise concentric circles to test how the various tube diameters would nest together. Once the internal clearances and wall thicknesses were locked in, I converted the layout into a solid, compact shaft. This solid representation maps out the collapsed state of the lightsaber, ensuring all nested layers fit tightly and efficiently within the footprint of the hilt.

Next, I created an assembly workspace to test the mechanical extension of the blade. By running a virtual extension test, I could check the overall reach and verify that the overlap ratios between stages would provide enough rigidity. Reviewing the wireframe assembly view confirmed that the internal stops and clearance margins line up properly as each segment slides outward. This simulation gave me the green light, proving that the physical model would telescope smoothly without binding or coming apart.

![Saber extend test](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/e4c92cb9870bb4a0cc9980bc0f7c6f945de8dab2503e2a318619f679b82e5dcc.png)

![saber extend ghost](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/ec426a858e76e8d90e08b558369e55762ce840c408cdc2c54d80b1a3139a618a.png)

The final major milestone was optimizing the manufacturing process. Instead of modeling and printing each tube individually, I refined the file into a single part design where all the slots and layers can be printed in one go. By keeping the print tolerances tight yet functional, the entire nested structure prints as a single assembly right off the bed. Once finished, it collapses smoothly and is immediately ready to be mounted straight into the custom hilt.

### 2026-10-16 – Transitioning from the internal blade mechanism to the exterior casing, I began drafting the lightsaber hilt in SolidWorks. Designing the hilt turned out to be far more difficult than anticipated; bal

**2h**

Transitioning from the internal blade mechanism to the exterior casing, I began drafting the lightsaber hilt in SolidWorks. Designing the hilt turned out to be far more difficult than anticipated; balancing ergonomic grip ribs, a faceted pommel base, and an angled emitter cutout required extensive trial and error. Looking at the initial wireframe layout and the final rendered solid model, capturing all those distinct aesthetic and structural features was a genuine struggle, but through sheer persistence, this is what I ultimately managed to build.

Just as I thought the assembly was coming together, a critical flaw became apparent: the hilt was simply too small to look and feel right. I had to pivot and use significantly larger dimensions to ensure proper proportions. Unfortunately, because the hilt scale and internal clearances changed so drastically, my previous work on the telescoping mechanism is no longer compatible. This means I have to completely scrap the old layout and redesign the extending shaft part from the very beginning to accommodate the new, larger hilt specifications for the event.

### 2026-10-16 – ![Saber shaft  final](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/865f3f8f92d95bc04a49f3bd64b4dfa2e82a6d6abeaa01288bf9cc1566647096.png)

**1h**

![Saber shaft  final](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/865f3f8f92d95bc04a49f3bd64b4dfa2e82a6d6abeaa01288bf9cc1566647096.png)

Following the setback with the initial hilt scaling, I completely rebuilt the telescoping shaft from scratch to match the larger, newly proportioned hilt dimensions. Re-architecting the concentric layers to fit the new scale required careful adjustments to tolerances and wall thicknesses, ensuring the print-in-place mechanics would still function flawlessly. As seen in the final assembly view, the newly scaled collapsible blade now nests securely and neatly inside the finished hilt body.

Looking back across the entire workflow—from the initial spark of childhood nostalgia and hand-drawn length calculations, through the trials of SolidWorks wireframes and simulation tests, to overcoming the hilt sizing hurdle—this project has been an intense exercise in iterative design. The complete CAD assembly successfully bridges the gap between old memories and modern 3D printing engineering. With the telescoping mechanics fully integrated, the proportions corrected, and the parts optimized, the lightsaber is now fully modeled and ready for production just in time
